messages.subject: Memory and speed for an LDA model
parts:
Hello folks,

I'm trying to test some adaptions of the latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) model, adaptions where collapsed Gibbs sampling isn't going to work right out of the box; I thought I'd try using a general purpose sampler, and STAN looked like it might be the best option in terms of speed. To begin, I coded up a version of standard LDA in stan (see below) and it seems to be working in very small data sets. However, if I push the number of text/size of the vocabulary to anything approaching what I'd need for a real world application, STAN quickly uses up all the memory on my server (92 Gigs!) and crashes, before the sampling processes even begins. I can scale it down a bit to the point where it has enough memory to start sampling, but I started a 50 text corpus a few days ago and its still running. This is much worse than the other general-purpose sampler I've tried (pymc). Anyway, I thought I'd check to see if maybe the problem was in my code, otherwise I have to reluctantly conclude that STAN (and general-purpose sampling in general) is not what I need, and I might as well go back to trying to hack existing LDA implementations for my purposes, which is not ideal:(. If anyone has any advice, specific or general, it would be much appreciated.

(Note: I don't sample the hyperparameters, instead I pass them in. Beta is a matrix of vectors so that I can use it to seed topics with specific words; Also, the entire corpus is a single vector, with switches between documents stored in a separate matrix (doc_ind); oh, and I have to add 1 to topic because categorical gives a range starting with zero whereas arrays start with 1, this mismatch seems like a bad design choice BTW)

data {
 int<lower=1> K; //topics
 int<lower=1> V; //vocabulary
 int<lower=1> D; //number of documents
 int<lower=1> T; // total number of words
 vector[K] alpha;
 vector[V] beta[K];
 
 int words[T];
 int doc_ind[D];
}

parameters {
simplex[V] psi[K];
simplex[K] theta[D];
}

model {
int start;
int topic;
for (n in 1:K) {
psi[n] ~ dirichlet(beta[n]);
}
for (n in 1:D) {
theta[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
}
start <- 1;
for (i in 1:D) {
for (j in start:doc_ind[i] - 1) {
topic ~ categorical(theta[i]);
words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic + 1]);
}
start <- doc_ind[i];
}
 
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
parts:
We don't really recommend Stan for models like LDA.
The problem is that the multi-modality of the posterior
makes Bayesian inference intractable, not just for Stan,
but for any known technique.

That being the case, you might as well go for an optimizer.
Like the very scalable online one Matt (the inventor of
our sampler, NUTS) wrote for Vowpal Wabbit:

http://hunch.net/~vw/

and described in this paper:

http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/HoffmanBleiBach2010b.pdf

The reason Stan's consuming so much memory is that we're
building up the log probability expression tree in memory to
use to compute auto-diff.

I believe PyMC uses Metropolis, which may run and provide
samples, but isn't going to give you very efficient sampling,
even around a single mode.

Finally, the Stan model isn't well formed because
we don't do integer sampling. So the "topic ~ categorical(...)"
isn't going to do what you think -- what it will do is
add log categorical(topic|theta[i]) to the log probabilty
where topic is uninitialized.

What you need to do is marginalize out the discrete
variables because Stan doesn't sample them. Here's
a note on how to do that for basic LDA:

http://lingpipe-blog.com/2011/04/14/summing-out-topic-assignments-ld/

This can also be a useful move if you're applying some
kind of optimization.

> model {
> int start;
> int topic;
> for (n in 1:K) {
> psi[n] ~ dirichlet(beta[n]);
> }
> for (n in 1:D) {
> theta[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
> }
> start <- 1;
> for (i in 1:D) {
> for (j in start:doc_ind[i] - 1) {
> topic ~ categorical(theta[i]);
> words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic + 1]);
> }
> start <- doc_ind[i];
> }
> }

Also, I don't follow the use of start here. Why not
write this loop as in the Blei et al. LDA paper? That is,
as:

for (d in 1:D) {
theta[d] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
for (j in 1:N[d]) {
topic[j] ~ categorical(theta[d]);
words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic[j]]);
}
}

The indexing in Stan is from 1, by the way, so I doubt
you wanted the +1 inside of psi.

You'd also need an index, as in topic[j], if we
supported discrete sampling. At least the above is how
I'd write it in BUGS/JAGS (modulo their matrix slicing
syntax which I can never remember).

- Bob

parts:
Ah, so a number of issues. Oddly, the compiler was giving me errors that made me think that categorical was doing what I wanted (e.g. saying topic was in the wrong range, e.g. 0-9 instead of 1-10, when I added 1 it stopped complaining) but I guess not. But even if I get rid of that topic selection categorical (which I actually did in my pymc implementation, now that I think about it), is the other one (the one that picks the words) kosher? Can't do LDA without something categorical, I wouldn't think...

Am I wrong in thinking that STAN can't deal with 2-dimensional objects where the second dimension is of varying length? That's why I don't just iterate over documents, instead I iterate over document end indices, and then over a range in the single corpus vector they point to. Start is really just there so I don't get an out-of-range error on the first iteration, though now that I think about it I could get rid of it by fixing my data.

Anyway, the bigger issue is performance, I guess STAN isn't the right thing from that perspective. Which is too bad, because it would be perfect otherwise; the problem with an off-the-shelf LDA solution is that I don't care about LDA specifically, I just want to test out some models which are similar to see if they work for my particular application, and I'd love to be able to fiddle at the exactly the level of abstraction provided in STAN (or other samplers, though I was particularly taken with STAN's detailed, well-written docs, thumbs up on that). I'm not much of a low-level programmer nor a statistics guru, so making collapsed gibbs sampling or any other optimization work for the actual models I have in mind (if even possible) is a slightly daunting prospect. But I think I'm finally convinced that's the only way to proceed.

BTW, Bob, we're actually acquainted, I met you briefly when you visited the UofT CL group a while back, unfortunately Gibbs sampling wasn't on my radar yet then, or you might have warned me away then. Thanks, everyone, for the info.

Julian

On Monday, October 8, 2012 4:51:58 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
We don't really recommend Stan for models like LDA.
The problem is that the multi-modality of the posterior
makes Bayesian inference intractable, not just for Stan,
but for any known technique.

That being the case, you might as well go for an optimizer.
Like the very scalable online one Matt (the inventor of
our sampler, NUTS) wrote for Vowpal Wabbit:

   http://hunch.net/~vw/

and described in this paper:

   http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/HoffmanBleiBach2010b.pdf

The reason Stan's consuming so much memory is that we're
building up the log probability expression tree in memory to
use to compute auto-diff.

I believe PyMC uses Metropolis, which may run and provide
samples, but isn't going to give you very efficient sampling,
even around a single mode.

Finally, the Stan model isn't well formed because
we don't do integer sampling.  So the "topic ~ categorical(...)"
isn't going to do what you think -- what it will do is
add log categorical(topic|theta[i]) to the log probabilty
where topic is uninitialized.

What you need to do is marginalize out the discrete
variables because Stan doesn't sample them.  Here's
a note on how to do that for basic LDA:

http://lingpipe-blog.com/2011/04/14/summing-out-topic-assignments-ld/

This can also be a useful move if you're applying some
kind of optimization.

 > model {
 > int start;
 > int topic;
 > for (n in 1:K) {
 > psi[n] ~ dirichlet(beta[n]);
 > }
 > for (n in 1:D) {
 > theta[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
 > }
 > start <- 1;
 > for (i in 1:D) {
 >   for (j in start:doc_ind[i] - 1) {
 >     topic ~ categorical(theta[i]);
 >     words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic + 1]);
 >   }
 >   start <- doc_ind[i];
 > }
 > }

Also, I don't follow the use of start here.  Why not
write this loop as in the Blei et al. LDA paper?  That is,
as:

for (d in 1:D) {
   theta[d] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
   for (j in 1:N[d]) {
     topic[j] ~ categorical(theta[d]);
     words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic[j]]);
   }
}

The indexing in Stan is from 1, by the way, so I doubt
you wanted the +1 inside of psi.

You'd also need an index, as in topic[j], if we
supported discrete sampling.  At least the above is how
I'd write it in BUGS/JAGS (modulo their matrix slicing
syntax which I can never remember).

- Bob

Stan can be used to fit LDA. But you may be disappointed if you compare its ability to find good parameters quickly with a standard collapsed Gibbs sampler.

CGS is a really surprisingly good stochastic search algorithm for LDA—it seems to be much easier to optimize the log-likelihood in "z-space" (the word-topic assignments) than in "theta-phi-space" (the topics and topic weights). One reason is sparsity—if you use Dirichlet priors with small hyperparameters and sum out the z variables (which you need to in Stan), then you wind up with a highly nonconvex sparsity-inducing prior. Gradient-based optimization on these kinds of nonconvex problems is very, very hard, and since NUTS relies very heavily on the use of gradient information to tell it where to explore, it's challenging for it to figure out what topics should be active in what documents. (Although in principle it'll figure it out eventually.)

What NUTS is good at is mixing quickly and delivering large numbers of effectively independent samples. Nobody really knows what the mixing speed of CGS is like, and most people don't care—for most topic modeling applications people aren't really interested in quantifying the uncertainty in their parameter estimates.

Matt

I'm a researcher, so uncertainty matters to me because producing just a point estimate wouldn't be acceptable for publication (for good reason, IMHO). It looks like I could "hack" either of those packages to call them repeatedly but the mixing across such iterations may just be so poor that NUTS would be faster. More importantly, neither lda or topicmodels is designed to accommodate prior information on how the word distribution differs across topics -- both have just a single parameter for beta (as well as alpha) but my prior knowledge is in how beta differs across topics. Recall that this was my strategy for navigating the multi-modality problems that Bob mentioned (I should be able to keep increasing the strength of my priors until the posterior becomes unimodal). To give you more specific detail on my particular problem: my purpose is to estimate the share of each topic discussed in each of 50 documents. I have 50 to 100 pre-determined topics (they are industry names taken from NAICS codes, such as "Oil and Gas Extraction") to which I add an additional topic I call "misc" for none of the above. From these topic descriptions, I have constructed my 1000 to 4000 word vocabulary (e.g. it contains "oil", "gas", "extraction", "oil extraction", and "gas extractrion"). In setting the prior on beta, I can make it so that the word "oil" is more probable than other words when the topic is "oil and gas extraction" (I might have to experiment with how strong it needs to be to ensure that the term "oil" is most associated with "oil and gas extraction", which is what I meant by making the posterior unimodal).   int <lower = 2> V;                // Num Words in Vocabulary
  int <lower = 1> M;                // Num Docs
  int <lower = 0> K[V,M];           // search term counts in each of the M docs
  vector <lower = 0> [T] alpha[M];  // topic prior
  vector <lower = 0> [V] beta[T];   // word prior
}
parameters{
  simplex [T] theta[M]; // topic distribution for each of the M docs
  simplex [V] phi[T]; // word distribution for each of the T topics

}
model{
  for (m in 1:M)

theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha[m]);  //prior
  for (t in 1:T)
    phi[t] ~ dirichlet(beta[t]);     //prior
  for (v in 1:V) {
    for (m in 1:M) {
      real gamma [T];
      for (t in 1:T)
        gamma[t] <- log(theta[m,t]) + log(phi[t,v]); //likelihood
      increment_log_prob(K[v,m]*log_sum_exp(gamma));
    }
  }

library(rstan)
library(reshape2)

##### Import data files
Search.Term.Counts <- read.csv("string_title_year_count.csv")
Industry.Terms <- read.csv("search_terms_and_industries.csv")

# data cleaning: restrict to year 2012 and remove a few negative counts (probably due to a coding mistake upstream)
Search.Term.Counts.t <- subset(Search.Term.Counts,year==2012)
Search.Term.Counts.t$count <- ifelse(Search.Term.Counts.t$count < 0, 0, Search.Term.Counts.t$count)

# extract Num.Words.In.Vocabulary and Num.Docs from Search.Term.Counts 
Num.Words.In.Vocabulary <- length(levels(Search.Term.Counts.t$string))
Num.Docs <- length(levels(as.factor(Search.Term.Counts.t$title)))

# extract Num.Topics [= Num.Industries + 1] from Industry.Terms
Num.Topics <- length(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)))+1

# extract Search.Term.Counts
melted.Search.Term.Counts <- melt(Search.Term.Counts.t[,c("title","string","count")], id=c("title", "string"))
Search.Term.Counts.Array <- acast(melted.Search.Term.Counts, string ~ title)

# Create the simply flat topic prior 
# alpha here represents the virtual count of times we've seen this topic for this doc (akin to the beta distribution's parameters so that 1 is a flat uniform)
# Steyvers n Griffiths (2007) suggest 50/T, which is actually around 1 here anyway

rownames(Topic.Prior) <- c(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)),"000")
colnames(Topic.Prior) <- levels(as.factor(Search.Term.Counts.t$title))

# Create the topic prior which is flat but to which I'll add additional weight allocated for search terms known to be associated with particular industries
# beta here represents the virtual count of times we've seen this word used in this topic 
# Steyvers n Griffiths (2007) suggest 0.01, which is improper, but they acknowledge that it should depend on vocabulary, num docs, etc... so I'll stick with 1 that corresponds to a flat uniform
Word.Prior <- matrix(1,nrow=Num.Words.In.Vocabulary, ncol=Num.Topics)
rownames(Word.Prior) <- levels(Search.Term.Counts.t$string)
colnames(Word.Prior) <- c(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)),"000")

# add information to the word prior
# loop thru each industry (not including the misc topic category)
# find the maximum number of words in that industry's search terms
# loop thru that industry's search terms to appropriately increment the prior for cases of individual terms in a search string of multiple words:
# the individual word should be more associated with misc and the whole search string of multiple words should be more associated with the industry 
for (Current.Industry.Index in 1:(ncol(Word.Prior)-1)) {
  Industry.Code <- colnames(Word.Prior)[Current.Industry.Index]
  Current.Industry.Terms <- subset(Industry.Terms,code == Industry.Code)
  Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms <- sapply(gregexpr("\\W+", Current.Industry.Terms$string), function(x) sum(x>0) ) + 1
  Max.Num.Terms <- max(Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms)
  for (Current.String.Index in 1:nrow(Current.Industry.Terms)) {
    if (as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]) %in% rownames(Word.Prior)) {
      Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),Industry.Code] <- Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),Industry.Code] + Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms[Current.String.Index]
      Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),"000"] <- Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),"000"] + (Max.Num.Terms - Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms[Current.String.Index])
    }
  }
}

##########################################################################################

StanInputData <- list(T = Num.Topics, V = Num.Words.In.Vocabulary, M = Num.Docs, K = Search.Term.Counts.Array, alpha = t(Topic.Prior), beta = t(Word.Prior))

# run stan on the file, compile to C [stanc()], and iteratively draw samples from the posterior [sampling()]
stan.fit <- stan(file="LDA.stan", data=StanInputData, seed = 12345, iter=1000, chains=4)

I'm rather certain that each document includes more than 1 topic, although perhaps not every topic appears in each document... So, it still seems to me that LDA is the most appropriate model among those of which I'm aware...

I didn't run out of memory. This takes up about 1GB of memory, of which I still have 10GB free. Interestingly, when I look at the CPU usage of the core handling the process, it reads as only 80% busy...

Theta is the parameter of interest for me; the beta parameters are basically just "nuisance" parameters for my purposes. I want the prior on theta to be completely flat, hence me setting alpha = 1 for all topics. I'm not sure why that construction would save computation time since either way alpha = 1 for all topics and documents...

Yeah, I may have to resort to coding the [fast] CGS myself... or grab someone else's C code and embed it in-line within my r script...

parts: > I'm a researcher, so uncertainty matters to me because producing just a point estimate wouldn't be acceptable for publication (for good reason, IMHO).

Given that mixing across the combinatorially explosive number of modes for a model like LDA is impossible, any estimate of posterior uncertainty you wind up with is likely to be at best a very loose lower bound. As Bob said, the source of this multimodality is not just label-switching, but also the sparsity induced by the Dirichlet distribution. Reporting posterior-based confidence intervals may therefore be more misleading than not including any confidence intervals at all.

Perhaps you can describe the specific question you're trying to answer and get uncertainty estimates about?

Theta is the parameter of interest for me; the beta parameters are basically just "nuisance" parameters for my purposes. I want the prior on theta to be completely flat, hence me setting alpha = 1 for all topics.

FYI, this isn't an "uninformative" prior. Like all priors on the simplex, it corresponds to a very specific set of assumptions about how many topics you expect to see per document.

A less rigid approach would be to learn the prior on theta, as suggested by Wallach et al. in "Rethinking LDA: Why Priors Matter":
https://people.cs.umass.edu/~wallach/publications/wallach09rethinking.pdf

Matt

You're right, I'd want to be clear about that. I thought that my prior scheme would also rule out the sparsity-induced multi-modality. If every Dirichlet parameter is greater than or equal to 1 then it should be unimodal in the simplex. Again, I could be missing something...

Matt, I sent you a private email about my particular application, which is unlikely to be of interest to the broader user group...

Yeah, if the Dirichlet parameters are all equal to 1, then the prior is uniform in the simplex. Such an assumption increases the appeal of Bayesian work to an audience dominated by frequentists because it makes the posterior proportional to the data's likelihood (with which they are comfortable). However, you're right that any prior corresponds to a very specification set of assumptions about how many topics we'd expect to see (a priori) in a document. Hence, flat isn't exactly uninformative, which can be seen via a reparameterization of the model. 

I found the approach proposed by Wallach et al. (2009), ie optimization with respect to the prior parameters, to be rather appealing; however, I didn't immediately understand the intuition behind their results. I would have thought that the (abstract) symmetry in the problem would result in the symmetric-asymmetric prior being just as good as the asymmetric-symmetric prior. That said, if I tried to wholely adopt their recommended approach, then I would lose the ability to incorporate my prior information (which, intuitively, is the whole purpose of a prior) and I may not be able to cleanly assign the pre-determined topic names to the latent topics generated... By the way, I noticed that this Wallach et al. I'd suggest doing a sensitivity analysis with different priors.
They make a huge difference in terms of the implicit correlation
among words being modeled. High count priors in alpha spread
out each document, which in effect shrinks all the topic models
and lessens the correlation effect in the posterior.

LDA's pretty good at modeling the burstiness of words across
documents, but you'll need to tune the priors heavily if you
expect it to be well calibrated to new data in the language
modeling sense of making good predictions (high probability) for
new documents.

> I'm rather certain that each document includes more than 1 topic, although perhaps not every topic appears in each document... So, it still seems to me that LDA is the most appropriate model among those of which I'm aware...

I often see people use alpha << 1 to avoid the following issue.

Suppose you have 100 words in a document and 100 topics.
And you see 10 words in one topic, 30 in a second, and
60 in a third. Then you get 11/200, 31/200, and 61/200
posterior mean probabilities and about half the posterior
mass assigned to the 97 "out-of-topic" topics.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
parts:
> On Jan 12, 2016, at 8:58 PM, stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Other than for playing around with models, I'd think a custom
> LDA fitter would make more sense. It's not like you can do
> real Bayesian inference with LDA anyway --- the posterior is
> combinatorially intractable.

> So, are you saying that Stan, BUGS, JAGS are not suitable for any LDA implementation? What could be an example of a custom
> LDA fitter?

What I'm saying is that you can't do Bayesian inference
for LDA. Nobody can do Bayesian inference for LDA --- there
are too many modes in the posterior.

The best an MCMC algorithm can do for LDA is explore around a single
mode. So if you start multiple chains, they'll never converge to
the same answer with realistic data (at least any kind of natural
language data I've ever seen). Now there's some stability in
the major clusters found, as analyzed by Griffiths and Steyvers
for their Gibbs sampler (which marginalizes out the continuous
parameters).

So what I'm saying is that you might as well use something like
variational inference and be content with a single mode. Or
just a point estimate. You'll find a super-scalable stochastic
variational inference implemented by Matt Hoffman (who also invented
the NUTS algorithm we use in Stan's MCMC) in Vowpal Wabbit.
Here's the writeup:

http://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/v14/hoffman13a.html

- Bob
